strengths: Introduces a novel and well-motivated threat model (Erasure Evasion Backdoors) that unifies data-based and weight-based backdoor injection to circumvent concept erasure, filling a clear gap since prior work studied backdoors and erasure largely in isolation.

Extensive empirical evaluation spanning three tasks (celebrity/personal-rights erasure, object erasure, explicit-content erasure), six erasure methods including three that explicitly claim adversarial robustness (RECE, RECELER, AdvUnlearn), two model families/architectures (SD v1.4, SD v2.1) plus a preliminary extension to the DiT-based FLUX model, which strengthens generality claims.

The proposed EEB_deep score-based attack is a reasonably principled construction (self-distillation with trigger/quality/retention losses) and is shown via ablations (Table 8, Table 9, Fig. 10) to be necessary in its components and to have been tuned sensibly (e.g., iteration count, alpha weighting).

Goes beyond just demonstrating the attack: includes trajectory analysis across erasure iterations (Supp. C), multi-trigger and multi trigger-target experiments (Supp. E), and a defense/detectability discussion (WeightWatcher weight-deviation diagnostics, T2IShield activation monitoring) that partially mitigates the paper being purely offensive.

Good reproducibility effort: detailed supplementary material describing hyperparameters, official implementations used for baselines, prompt templates, computational cost breakdown, and a stated commitment to release code/templates and a responsible disclosure timeline for full model checkpoints.
Clear framing of ethical considerations (censored explicit content, impact statement, discussion of responsible disclosure) appropriate for a dual-use security paper.
weaknesses: The core threat model requires the adversary to have released/poisoned the model or training data before erasure is applied, and for defenders to then obtain and use that exact poisoned model unmodified; the practical likelihood and typical pipeline for this scenario (e.g., why a safety-conscious deployer would fine-tune/erase directly on an untrusted third-party checkpoint without further vetting) is not deeply justified or discussed relative to more standard backdoor threat models.

The white-box EEB_deep variant assumes an adversary with substantial control over U-Net fine-tuning (LoRA across all layers) and knowledge that the model owner will apply concept erasure afterward and not further fine-tune/train on curated data; this fairly strong and specific assumption is somewhat inconsistent with the more constrained EEB_surface/shallow variants and the differing feasibility across variants is not always foregrounded when synthesizing headline numbers in the abstract (e.g., 'up to 94%' figures likely stem from the strongest, least realistic white-box variant).

The detectability/defense discussion (Section 4.6) is comparatively brief and mostly qualitative (a single AUC figure for T2IShield, general remarks about WeightWatcher deviations); no proposed or evaluated concrete mitigation method is offered beyond citing existing detectors, leaving the 'potential remedies' promised in the contributions list underdeveloped.

Some results show non-monotonic or inconsistent trends (e.g., RECE/RECELER sometimes reducing target exposure post-EEB in explicit-content erasure, ESD-X's own baseline high target-recognition rates confounding interpretation in Table 11) that are acknowledged but not fully resolved, slightly complicating the clean narrative of universal EEB success.

The paper relies on a single detector (GCD) for celebrity identification and NudeNet for explicit content as ground truth for ASR; classifier errors/biases could affect the reported numbers, and no human evaluation or cross-validation with a second classifier is reported to corroborate automated metrics.

FLUX experiments (Section 4.5) are limited to only two erasure methods (ESD, UCE) and lack the full breadth (RECE/RECELER/AdvUnlearn, object/explicit-content tasks) applied to SD, so claims of cross-architecture generality are only partially substantiated.

strengths: Introduces a conceptually interesting and underexplored intersection between backdoor poisoning and concept-erasure robustness, framing a concrete new threat model (EEB) with black-box and three levels of white-box variants (surface/shallow/deep).

Very extensive empirical evaluation: three application scenarios (celebrity identity, object erasure, explicit content), six erasure baselines including three methods explicitly claiming adversarial robustness (RECE, RECELER, AdvUnlearn), three base architectures (SD v1.4, SD v2.1, FLUX), plus trajectory analysis, trigger-choice studies, multiple simultaneous backdoors, and detectability/defense experiments (weight anomaly detection, T2IShield prompt detection).

Results are reasonably consistent across settings and show a real gap: even erasure methods that search for adversarial representations of the target concept fail to remove the deep (EEB_deep) backdoor link, which is a non-trivial and somewhat surprising finding.

Paper is transparent about limitations, ethical considerations (censoring explicit content, responsible disclosure plan for code/checkpoints), and explicitly positions EEB as a diagnostic/stress-testing tool rather than only an attack, which is a constructive framing.
Good appendix with algorithmic details, ablations on loss terms and the alpha hyperparameter, and computational cost reporting, which aids understanding of the design choices.
weaknesses: The core novel attack (EEB_deep) is methodologically incremental: it is essentially a teacher-student distillation objective with an added trigger-conditioned loss, LoRA fine-tuning, and standard retention/quality regularizers—conceptually similar to existing backdoor-injection and unlearning techniques rather than a fundamentally new mechanism.

The threat model's practical significance is debatable: it requires either an adversary with white-box access who poisons a model prior to publication, or contamination of pretraining data, with the defender then blindly applying erasure to an untrusted checkpoint. This is a narrower scenario than generic 'erasure fails against adversarial prompts' vulnerabilities (e.g., Pham et al., Zhang et al.) already documented, and the paper does not clearly quantify how much of its contribution goes beyond these known prompt-level circumvention results when no poisoning is used.

The paper's own detectability analysis (Section 4.6, Fig. 7-8) shows that EEB_shallow leaves strong weight-level traces and that EEB_deep triggered prompts are separable by existing detectors (T2IShield AUC ~90%), yet no end-to-end experiment combines such defenses with erasure to show whether the overall pipeline (detection + erasure) still fails—this would be the most convincing test of real-world significance and is missing.

Several results are averaged over a small number of targets/triggers (e.g., 2-3 celebrities, one representative trigger per category) with visibly large variance (wide shaded bands in Fig. 9, inconsistent trends such as ESD-X's erratic ASR curve), raising concerns about the statistical robustness of some comparative claims.

Full code and poisoned checkpoints are withheld pending a 'responsible disclosure timeline,' with only a minimal codebase promised for reviewers, which limits independent reproducibility verification at review time despite the otherwise detailed methodological descriptions.

Presentation relies heavily on dense tables and small, censored qualitative figures (Fig. 4-6), making it hard to independently judge the severity/quality of circumvented content; some claims (e.g., 'up to 16x amplification') are headline numbers from best-case cells rather than representative central tendencies, which could overstate the general threat level.

strengths: Introduces a novel and timely threat model (Erasure Evasion Backdoors) that connects two previously separate lines of research—backdoor attacks and concept erasure—revealing that erasure methods can fail to remove maliciously embedded trigger-target links even when they appear to succeed on standard benchmarks.

Very comprehensive empirical evaluation: four attack variants spanning black-box data poisoning to white-box interventions at increasing depth (text encoder, cross-attention, full U-Net), tested against six erasure baselines including methods explicitly designed for adversarial robustness (RECE, Receler, AdvUnlearn), across three application scenarios (celebrity identity, object erasure, explicit content).

Generality is demonstrated across model families/architectures (SD v1.4, SD v2.1, and the DiT-based FLUX), strengthening the claim that the vulnerability is not specific to one erasure technique or backbone.

Extensive and careful ablation studies in the appendix (loss components, alpha weighting, trigger type sensitivity, training-iteration trajectories, multi-trigger and multi trigger-target settings) that support the robustness of the main findings and aid reproducibility.

The paper goes beyond simply demonstrating an attack by proposing EEB as a constructive diagnostic/stress-testing tool for future erasure methods, and it includes a thoughtful discussion of potential defenses (weight-deviation diagnostics, inference-time activation/prompt monitoring) and a responsible disclosure plan.

Clear, well-organized threat model formalization (surface/shallow/deep variants, black-box vs white-box access) that cleanly maps onto realistic adversarial capabilities (e.g., publishing poisoned checkpoints on open platforms).
weaknesses: The strongest and most consistent results come from EEB_deep, which requires substantial white-box access to modify U-Net parameters broadly; this is a fairly strong assumption, and the finding that such a pervasive, deeply embedded association is hard to erase is somewhat less surprising than the paper's framing suggests. The more "practical" surface and shallow (and even data-poisoning) variants show much weaker and inconsistent success against several erasure methods (e.g., EEB_surface often <10% ASR), which tempers the generality of the threat.

The black-box data-poisoning instantiation relies on fine-tuning a pretrained model with 1% contamination rather than demonstrating poisoning at web-scale pretraining time, which is acknowledged as a simplification but leaves open how effective/stealthy the attack would be in a true large-scale pretraining-data-poisoning scenario.

Evaluation relies heavily on automated classifiers (GCD celebrity classifier, CIFAR-10 ResNet, NudeNet) without human perceptual verification, which could introduce measurement bias or fail to capture whether erasure-evading generations are convincingly recognizable to humans.

The paper's own detectability analysis (Fig. 7, T2IShield AUC ≈ 90%) suggests that EEB-poisoned prompts/models are fairly distinguishable from clean ones, which somewhat undercuts the severity of the stealth claims made elsewhere in the paper; the trade-off between persistence and detectability could be discussed more thoroughly and quantitatively.

Results on multi-trigger/multi-target settings (Table 11, 12) show substantial variability—some trigger-target pairs fail to establish a reliable backdoor link at all—without a clear explanation of what makes certain triggers/targets more or less learnable, leaving some empirical findings under-explained.

The paper is dense with many notation variants (EEB_data/surface/shallow/deep, multiple accuracy subscripts) that, combined with the large volume of results spread across main text and lengthy appendices, somewhat hampers readability and makes it harder to extract the core takeaways without consulting supplementary material extensively.
